title: The Girl Who Crossed the Sea to Learn to Heal
shortDescription: She was married at nine and had never been to school. When her baby son died, she decided to become a doctor. She crossed the ocean, earned a medical degree in America, and came home to India. She died at twenty-one before she could use it.
heroImageCaption: Anandibai Joshee, M.D., class of 1886 · public domain
introduction: In 1878, in a town in western India, a fourteen-year-old girl held her baby son. He lived ten days. There was no trained doctor to call, and after he was gone the girl could not put down a question: who would care for Indian women when male doctors would not? Her name was Anandi Gopal Joshi. She had been married at nine to a postal clerk, and she had never gone to school. Five years later she stood before a crowd in Serampore and said India needed women doctors. Then she crossed the sea to learn how to become one. She came home with a medical degree. She never got to use it.

chapters.heading: A girl who kept asking
paragraphs: Anandi was born Yamuna Joshi on 31 March 1865 in Kalyan, in the western state of Maharashtra. Her father, Gunputrao Joshi, kept a schoolroom in a large room of their house. He was a teacher and a scholar. Yamuna was his sixth child. She spent her happiest hours on his knee under a plane tree in the garden. She was small, and she watched everything. One day she saw a priest wash and oil an idol. An idol is a statue used in worship. 'Papa,' she asked, 'how can a god bear to have his face washed by a man?' Her father told her the statue was only a way to hold the mind on God. She did not argue. She simply decided she would never wash an idol's face herself.

Before she was five, she told her father about a dream. An armed ancestor had come to her and said she would walk in his footsteps. Caroline Dall, the American writer who later recorded her life, wrote that her father opened the family record after that and began to take her education seriously. It is a small thing, but it changed the shape of her days. A girl in that time was often kept from books. Her father let her learn.

When Yamuna was five, a man named Gopal Vinayak Joshi became a postal clerk in Bombay. He was a widower and much older than she was. He came to the house and taught her Sanskrit, an old Indian language used in religious books, for nearly three years. Then he was promoted and moved to Alibag, a town by the sea. The lessons stopped. Years later she told Dall that she thought she would never learn anything more, and that she would rather have died. That is how much those lessons meant to her.

In those years she learned the habits that stayed with her for life. She wore bangles, or stiff bracelets, on her arms and anklets on her feet. She marked her forehead each day. She knew the family prayers and songs. When she crossed the ocean later, she carried these small customs with her like a home she could fold and take out. A child who asks why is never quite happy with the answer she is given. Yamuna kept asking.

chapters.heading: The child who lived ten days

media.alt: Photograph of Anandi Gopal Joshi taken before 1887
media.caption: Anandi Gopal Joshi, photographed before 1887.
media.credit: Purnima Varman (uploader) / Columbia University — Public domain

paragraphs: On 31 March 1874, on her ninth birthday, Yamuna married Gopal Joshi. He gave her a new name, Anandabai. Dall says it meant 'joy of my heart.' In those days a girl of nine could be married to a man much older than herself, and there was no one to ask whether she was ready. In the stories she told, Gopal was her teacher. He had taught her Sanskrit. Now he taught her other things, and he expected her to learn them fast.

In early 1878, at fourteen, she had a baby boy. He lived about ten days. We do not know his name. We know what she said about him years later, and the words are plain enough: 'A child's death does no harm to its father, but its mother does not want it to die.' In the place where they lived, no trained doctor could save him. That loss turned into a question. If Indian women would not be seen by male doctors, who would care for them when they gave birth?

She did not have a school, a fee, or a plan. She had a grief and a question. Over the next months, the question became a decision. She would go to America and learn to be a doctor herself. It was not a small thing to say out loud in a country where a woman who crossed the sea was spoken of with fear. But she had already learned that a closed door can be opened by someone who keeps standing in front of it.

chapters.heading: An answer from New Jersey

media.alt: Photograph of Anandi Gopal Joshi with her signature
media.caption: A photograph of Anandi with her signature, made before 1887.
media.credit: Unknown photographer / Columbia University — Public domain

paragraphs: On 4 September 1878, Gopal wrote to a Presbyterian missionary in Kolhapur, a city in western India. Presbyterian is one branch of the Christian church. A missionary is a person who travels to tell others about their faith. His question was direct: could a Hindu woman study medicine in America? An American doctor named Wilder wrote back on 14 October. His answer was no. He did not want a Hindu woman who had not become a Christian to come. Gopal did not let that end the matter. In January 1879 his letter was printed in the Missionary Review, a magazine in Princeton, New Jersey.

In the spring of 1880, a woman named Theodicia Carpenter sat in a dentist's office in Elizabeth, New Jersey. She picked up an old copy of that magazine from a table. She read the letter and copied down the address. The next morning she felt she had to write. She wrote to Gopal in March 1880 and offered him and Anandi a home if they ever came to America. Anandi called her 'aunt.' The two women had never met, but letters began to cross the ocean between them.

Those letters were not just polite words. Theodicia wanted to understand the life Anandi came from. Anandi sent photographs. In one she stood bare-armed with many bracelets. In another her feet showed anklets and toe rings. There was a mark on her forehead. She explained each custom, and in doing so she had to put her own life into words. She was teaching her future friend how to see her. When she wrote that she wanted to keep her manners unless they harmed her health, she was drawing a line she would not cross.

By 1881 the family had moved often, to Kutch, to Calcutta, to Barrackpore. Anandi was sick for long stretches. She was carried to a friend's house to be nursed. In a letter from Serampore she said other women would not sit with her unless she became a missionary or forced her way into the zenana, the part of an Indian house where women lived apart from male visitors. She was being asked to give up who she was in order to be accepted. She kept the letters going. Each one made the plan more real.

chapters.heading: The crowd at Serampore
paragraphs: Serampore was a town near Calcutta. By early 1883, people there had begun to follow Anandi in the street. Some shouted questions. Some threw stones. At the post office, a crowd once gathered so thick that the public work could not go on. Christian leaders wanted her to be baptised before she went abroad. Brahmins, the Hindu priests, spoke against her for leaving at all. Both sides wanted her to be someone else before she was allowed to go.

Gopal offered to make the public statement for her. He thought it would be easier if a man spoke. Anandi said no. She would speak herself. On 24 February 1883, a hall in Serampore was full of Indian and European listeners. A clergyman named Summers led the meeting. She had no notes and had not prepared a speech. She stood up and told them why she was going. India needed Hindu women doctors, she said. There was a growing need for them, and she would qualify herself for one.

The crowd had questions of its own. Who are you? What caste do you belong to? Where do you come from? Where are you going? Caste is the social group a person is born into. She answered them. 'I am not going to America through any whim or caprice,' she said. A whim is a sudden wish. This was not that. 'Therefore I go alone.' The room heard a person who had thought about the cost. Afterward the head of the postal service, H. E. M. James, sent congratulations and a cheque for a hundred rupees.

That speech matters because it was hers. A girl who had been married at nine, who had no school of her own, stood in front of a hostile hall and explained her life. She did not ask them to agree. She told them what she meant to do. In the weeks that followed, her sailing was put off twice. On 3 April 1883 she wrote that she would go on board on the evening of the sixth and start the next morning. The wait was nearly over.

chapters.heading: The bangles that paid for the ship
paragraphs: On 7 April 1883, Anandi sailed from Calcutta for New York on a ship called the City of Calcutta. A saree is a long cloth wrapped around the body, and she wore hers with care. The women travelling with her were strangers. They were cold to her, and she later said she was under restraint. They doubted she would stay Hindu, and they felt it was their duty to press Christianity on her. In London she was asked to show her finest saree and jewels at missionary gatherings. She was being looked at, not met.

Years later, after her death, her family learned something she had never told them. The heavy bangles her father had given her at her marriage had been sold. The money had helped pay for the passage. She had gone without the bracelets she wore as a girl in order to buy a seat on a ship. There is no record of her speaking about it. The silence itself tells us how much she wanted this.

The sea crossing took months. She wrote letters at every port. She was going to a country where she knew almost no one, to study a subject that had been closed to Indian women. She had no degree, no money of her own, and a husband who moved them from town to town. What she had was a promise she had made to Dall: in America she would 'eat and drink, live or die as a Hindu.' Every mile of the voyage put that promise to the test.

chapters.heading: A Hindu in Roselle

media.alt: Anandi Joshee with fellow medical students Kei Okami and Tabat Islambooly
media.caption: Anandi Joshee (left) with Kei Okami of Japan and Tabat Islambooly of Ottoman Syria, students at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1885.
media.credit: Unknown photographer / Drexel University — Public domain

paragraphs: She reached New York on 4 June 1883. Theodicia Carpenter and her husband met her. For the summer she stayed with them in Roselle, New Jersey. She called it the happiest summer of her life. Each day she put scarlet paste on her forehead. She wrote to Gopal by every mail. She studied Sanskrit and sang Hindu songs. She went to Tiffany's, the New York shop, and she held a small Indian feast for eighteen guests. She laid out red and white squares on the floor, used Indian powders, and set attar, a perfume, on each guest's right hand. There was no cutlery. This was her way of making a strange place familiar.

An offer came from a college in New York that used homeopathy, a different kind of medicine. The place was free. She turned it down. She wanted the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia. In late September she arrived there. On 3 October 1883 she enrolled. The dean, Dr. Rachel Bodley, gave her a scholarship and held a reception for her. Anandi came in a crimson and gold saree, with a nose ring worn as a brooch and six pairs of bangles.

Her first room in Philadelphia had a smoky stove and her Indian brass vessels. She was lonely. 'I feel very lonesome,' she wrote. Dr. Bodley moved her into her own house. From there Anandi wrote a line that says more than a page of description: 'How kind the Americans are!' Dall recorded that she spoke seven languages, among them English, Sanskrit and Marathi. Dall also wrote that her English was exquisite. The girl who had been taught at home was now studying medicine beside women from other countries.

Those women became part of her story. In 1885 a photograph was taken of three students from the same college. On the left was Anandi, from India. In the centre was Kei Okami, from Japan. On the right was Tabat Islambooly, from Ottoman Syria. Each was the first woman from her country to earn a medical degree in the West. They had all travelled a long way to sit in the same classrooms. Anandi kept her customs while she learned her lessons. She did not treat the two as enemies.

chapters.heading: Fifty pages and a white saree

media.alt: Photograph of Anandi Gopal Joshi from Caroline Dall's book, mirrored on Wikimedia Commons
media.caption: Anandi Gopal Joshi, photographed before 1887. The copy on Wikimedia Commons is mirrored.
media.credit: Caroline Wells Healey Dall / Drexel University — Public domain (mirrored on Commons)

paragraphs: In February 1884 she caught diphtheria, a serious illness of the throat. Her life was briefly despaired of. Dr. Bodley and another doctor, Dr. Schultze, attended her. She recovered, but money was a constant worry. In October 1884 she wrote to Theodicia: 'I have not a cent with me, but owe a little to Mrs. Smith, and cannot get to clinics for the same reason. I have had a very severe cold for a week, and am aching all over.' She was ill, broke, and far from home. She kept going to class.

Part of her study was obstetrics, the care of women when they give birth. At a lecture she sat through the dissection of a baby, the cutting open of a body to study it. She told Dall it would have been better if it had not been a baby. That line is not a complaint about the work. It is a mother speaking. By Christmas 1885 she had written a thesis, a long paper on one subject, of about fifty pages on Hindu obstetrics. It was the longest thing she had ever written.

On 31 January 1886 she wrote to Theodicia about graduation. 'Do not buy me anything for my graduation. Your presence will make me more happy than any gift.' That winter she fell on ice and broke the bangles on her right arm. Gopal bought her a gold bracelet. She said the money would have been better spent on an instrument or a book. Her aunt came to the ceremony anyway. Anandi had asked for the one thing that could not be bought.

On 11 March 1886, at noon, she took her degree in the Green Room of the Academy of Music, a concert hall in Philadelphia. About three thousand people were there. Pandita Ramabai, an Indian scholar who had also crossed the sea, sat near the front with her child. Anandi wore a pure white saree with a wide gold border. Dall wrote that she walked forward to take her diploma without a quiver of her lips. She was the first Indian woman to earn a medical degree in the United States. A letter from Queen Victoria followed in July. The Queen said she had read the account of the graduation 'with much interest.'

chapters.heading: I have done all that I could
paragraphs: Even before she graduated, a job was waiting. On 10 March 1886 the chief minister of Kolhapur wrote to Dr. Bodley. He offered Anandi the post of Lady Doctor of Kolhapur. The pay was three hundred rupees a month, rising to five hundred after five years. A house was provided, and one passage paid. She would have charge of the women's wards at Albert Edward Hospital and would teach girls in medicine. It was the post she had imagined when her son died. On 18 April she replied. The seven conditions were mostly fine. The seventh troubled her. 'Never from those who are poor and depressed,' she wrote of fees. She meant it.

Queen Victoria's congratulations arrived in July. Then her body began to fail again. In May she had gone to a hospital in Boston as a guest, not as a doctor. By June she had given up hospital work to rest. Dall found her lying pale and quiet, and a few days later she could move again. In the autumn of 1886 she sailed for India. On the way she stopped at a school for Native American children and spent ten days in a women's hospital in Philadelphia. Pandita Ramabai brought her back to Roselle. She still believed the sea air and her own country would restore her.

They did not. On 26 February 1887, just after midnight, she died in Poonah, now called Pune, after a convulsion, a sudden shaking of the body. She was twenty-one. Her last audible words were: 'I have done all that I could.' Her family washed and dressed her in bright clothes and ornaments, and she was cremated on the following Sunday, in a funeral fire as Hindu custom asks. Ramabai wrote two days later that not a word of complaint or impatience had left her. She had spent her life being told what a woman like her could not do.

Gopal gathered her ashes against the wishes of her family. He took them to Poughkeepsie, New York, and had them buried there. The stone reads: 'First Brahmin woman to leave India to obtain an education.' He had wanted the world to see what she had done. She never worked in Kolhapur. She never saw a patient in the hospital that had offered her a room. What she left was a degree, a handful of letters, and a question she had answered with her whole short life: who will care for the women?

challenge: A child bride with no schooling had to fight for the right to study medicine abroad while her own community turned against her.
journey: A letter printed in an American magazine brought a stranger's help; a public speech in Serampore carried her across the ocean to a medical college in Philadelphia.
achievement: She earned a medical degree at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1886, the first Indian woman to do so in the United States.
impact: Her short life showed that Indian women could qualify as doctors, and her letters remain a record of a woman who kept her customs while she learned a new trade.
lesson: A question asked at a child's deathbed can become a life's work, even if that life is cut short before the work begins.
